Baroque concertos create contrast through use of tutti and solo sections, terraced dynamics and contrasting textures.
The three movements of a concerto contrast with each other, and often one or more use ritornello form.
This features a ritornello section that returns throughout.
keywords: a composition for a solo instrument with orchestral accompaniment
the accompaniment section of the Baroque orchestra, normally including harpsichord and a bass stringed instrument (e.g. cello)
a recurring passage in a piece of Baroque music
where dynamics change suddenly, rather than gradually
In a tutti passage the whole ensemble plays

1157.name: The concerto grosso
1157.outcome: I can analyse key features of the concerto grosso.
points: The concerto grosso is a type of Baroque concerto that includes more than one soloist.
The group of soloists is called the concertino. It usually has two or three performers, most commonly violin and cello.
The accompanying group is called the ripieno, normally based around strings and continuo.
The concertino and ripieno interact in different ways, creating contrast.
keywords: the name for the group of soloists in a concerto grosso
a type of Baroque concerto that includes more than one soloist
the name for the group of accompanying instruments in a concerto grosso

1158.name: The concerto in the Classical period
1158.outcome: I can identify key features of the Classical concerto and compose an idiomatic cadenza.
points: The Classical concerto uses a larger orchestra than Baroque, with no continuo and a broader range of solo instruments.
The first movement typically uses sonata form - exposition, development and recapitulation.
The texture is usually melody and accompaniment, with a melody based on balanced phrasing.
Cadenzas are an opportunity for soloists to show off their technical skill, with virtuosic playing in a free tempo.
keywords: where melodic phrases are equal length and complementary melodic shape (also called 'question and answer' form)
a solo section in a concerto in which the soloist plays in a virtuosic manner
a texture consisting of a melody with a clearly separate accompaniment
a common structure for a piece, based on an exposition, development and recapitulation

1160.name: The romantic concerto
1160.outcome: I can identify and describe the key musical features of the Romantic concerto, and the ways that it differs from the classical concerto.
points: The Romantic concerto mirrored many typical features of Romantic music.
These include more complex textures, chromatic harmony, a larger orchestra and an emphasis on intense, expressive music.
Many Romantic concertos are extremely difficult for soloists and are highly virtuosic.
Bruch’s Violin Concerto reflects many of these typical features.
keywords: a solo section in a concerto in which the soloist plays in a virtuosic manner
a note that is not part of the key or scale
a slight speeding up and slowing down of the tempo to show expression
music that shows off a performer’s technical skill

1161.name: The piano concerto through time
1161.outcome: I can identify similarities and differences between the piano concertos of the Classical and Romantic periods.
points: The piano became a very important instrument in Classical and Romantic concertos.
Its dynamic range, pitch range, expressive abilities and ability to play multiple layers attracted composers to it.
The piano concerto mirrored most of the trends of those periods, though there are some specific ways the piano is used.
These include accompanying orchestral melodies with chords and playing both melody and accompaniment together.
keywords: A group of notes from a chord played one after the other, either ascending or descending
a note that is not part of the key or scale
music which uses only notes that are based in the key (e.g. C major or F minor)
a melody that uses segments of a scale
In a tutti passage the whole ensemble plays

11803.name: The instruments and rhythms of Palestinian folk music
11803.outcome: I can identify some key instruments and understand some key rhythms in Palestinian folk music.
points: Arabic music has a long and complex history and is extremely varied.
Two key instruments in Palestinian folk music are the doumbek and oud.
The doumbek uses three sounds - doum (middle of the drum), tek (edge of the drum) and ka (ring finger on edge of drum).
Palestinian folk music uses a wazn, a rhythmic cycle or pattern. Maqsum and saidi are two examples of this.
keywords: a drum used in Arabic and Palestinian folk music; it is played with the hands and fingertips
a common wazn across the Middle East
a stringed instrument with 11 strings used in Arabic and Palestinian music; it is an early predecessor to the guitar
a specific upbeat wazn that uses fast rhythmic patterns
a repeating rhythmic cycle or pattern that forms the rhythmic basis of a composition

11805.name: Song, dance and maqam in Palestinian folk music
11805.outcome: I can understand some of the key forms of Palestinian music and can improvise using a maqam.
points: Palestinian folk music has many popular forms, many of which are performed for dance.
Ataaba is a popular song form in Palestine, and dabke is an important traditional form of dance across the region.
Traditional Palestinian and Arabic music is based on a maqam, which is a set of notes.
Each maqam is microtonal and includes seven notes. They are usually taught by ear. Bayati is a common maqam.
Performers improvise using the maqam, including in taqsim at the start of a performance.
keywords: If a melody is microtonal it uses notes in between the 12 notes of the Western scale. It uses intervals smaller than a semitone.
a traditional form of solo Palestinian love song that is often heard at weddings and other occasions
a type of folk dance; it can be performed with different styles of music
a set of notes, (like a scale) that forms the basis of a composition; it is microtonal and has seven notes
an improvised solo based on a maqam that introduces a piece of music

11806.name: Israeli folk music
11806.outcome: I can explain the cultural and historic context of Israeli folk music and its key musical features.
points: Israeli folk music is influenced by various global regions and has strong ties with Jewish folk music.
It is often used to accompany dance, in particular at celebrations and festive occasions in Israel.
The music is energetic, upbeat and has a strong rhythmic pulse for dancing to.
Its distinct sound comes from its use of off-beat chords, accelerando and ornamentation, including note bends.
Typical instruments include violin, clarinet and accordion.
keywords: when the tempo gradually speeds up
when a musician ‘bends’ the pitch of a note
when a performer decorates a melody with extra notes (e.g. trills, turns)

11807.name: Understanding Greek folk music
11807.outcome: I can identify key instruments in Greek folk music and perform the basic 7/8 rhythms of ‘Thalassaki Mou’.
points: Greek folk music includes both folk songs and music for dance.
It uses a mix of common Western instruments and traditional Greek instruments, including the bouzouki and defi.
Much Greek folk music uses irregular time signatures such as 5/8 and 7/8.
Kalamatianó is a type of Greek folk dance which is based in 7/8.
Usually 7/8 is counted as a 3-2-2. 5/8 is counted as 3-2.
keywords: a type of tambourine, a small hand drum with bangles
the number of beats cannot be divided by 2 or 3 (e.g. 5, 7)
a type of Greek folk dance which is based in 7/8 metre

11808.name: Melody in Greek folk music
11808.outcome: I can identify the typical features of melody in Greek folk music and perform them in Thalassaki Mou.
points: The bouzouki has a characteristic playing style that uses slides and tremolo.
Instrumental and vocal melodies are often harmonised with thirds.
Melodies in Greek folk music are mostly conjunct and use ornamentation.
The vocal melodies are often conjunct and melismatic, like in Thalassaki Mou.
keywords: movement between notes based on small intervals (steps)
when there are syllables with more than one note sung to them
To observe a specimen using a light microscope, we have to put a thin layer of it on a glass microscope slide.
an interval of three notes. When both notes are performed together, the harmony would be described as ‘3rds’
alternating between two notes rapidly; sounds like a trembling effect

5859.name: Fundamentals of melody
5859.outcome: I can describe basic features of melodies and different common methods of melodic development.
points: Melodies can be analysed by looking at melodic shape, intervals, repetition and contrast, motifs and phrases.
Most composers develop melodies to create a balance between repetition and contrast.
Adding notes and changing rhythms are simple ways to develop a melody.
Augmentation, diminution and sequences are also common methods for melodic development.
keywords: the process of lengthening all of the notes in a melody by the same proportion
the process of shortening all of the notes in a melody by the same proportion
a short section of a melody, often lasting 1, 2 or 4 bars
a short melodic idea that recurs throughout a piece of music
a short melodic idea that is repeated in steps either rising or falling

5860.name: Other melodic devices
5860.outcome: I can identify a range of common melodic devices, including ornamentation, imitation and countermelodies.
points: Composers use different melodic devices to develop and enhance their melodies.
Ornamentation is a common melodic device in many styles.
Common ornaments are trills, grace notes, turns and mordents.
Imitation is a device where a part of a melody is copied in another part immediately or shortly afterwards.
A countermelody is a contrasting second melody. It plays at the same time as the main melody and has equal prominence.
keywords: a second melody that plays at the same time as the main melody
a very fast note that plays just before a main melodic note: it is sometimes referred to as an acciaccatura
a melodic device in which part of the melody is copied immediately in another part
a type of ornamentation that creates the effect of a short trill
a type of ornamentation based on alternating rapidly between two notes

5862.name: Tonality and intervals
5862.outcome: I can describe and identify the different types of tonality, and can identify intervals in context.
points: Tonality determines the notes that are used in a piece of music.
Lots of Western music is diatonic or chromatic, while many traditional styles around the world are modal.
Atonal music has no key and microtonal music uses notes from in between the semitones.
Identifying intervals allows musicians to work out musical ideas by ear.
The simplest way to do this is by comparing intervals to reference songs.
keywords: If a melody is microtonal it uses notes in between the 12 notes of the Western scale. It uses intervals smaller than a semitone.
music which has no key or tonic note
a note that is not part of the key or scale
music which uses only notes that are based in the key (e.g. C major or F minor)
music based on a mode, a type of scale different from major and minor scales

5863.name: Chords and cadences
5863.outcome: I can identify different chord types by ear and through notation, and can identify different cadences.
points: Major triads, minor triads and extended chords can be identified by listening carefully to the feeling of each chord.
The tonic chord (I) can be identified by the ‘finished’ feeling that it creates.
The dominant (V) and subdominant (IV) chords can be identified by listening for the bass notes.
We can identify cadences by the feeling they create - perfect and plagal feel finished, imperfect and interrupted don’t.
Listening for the bass notes helps to distinguish between perfect (V-I) and plagal (IV-I) cadences.
keywords: a V-I progression at the end of a section of music; it feels resolved
the fifth note in a scale, or the chord based on that note (chord V)
where part of a chord sequence finishes on the dominant chord (V), which feels unfinished
chord I - the 'home' note and chord of a key and the note that the key is named after

5864.name: Harmonic devices
5864.outcome: I can identify a range of harmonic devices and how they are used.
points: Composers use various common harmonic devices to enhance harmony and create certain musical effects.
Drones, pedals and ground bass are all determined by the bass parts and how they relate to the chords.
Modulations are changes in key that can radically alter the mood of a piece of music.
Suspensions are a specific type of dissonance that is used to create harmonic tension and resolution.
keywords: a constant, pitched sound that continues throughout a piece of music
a short, repeated bass line that repeats throughout a piece, forming the structure of the music
a change of key during a piece of music
a continuous pitch or note in the music which remains the same as the other harmonies change
A mixture of an insoluble solid and liquid in which the solid particles are dispersed in the liquid and settle upon the mixture standing.

7452.name: Understanding timbre: Western sounds
7452.outcome: I can identify common instruments and timbres from different Western musical traditions.
points: The orchestra is home to a diverse range of instruments which use different effects to create different timbres.
Some common effects include: arco, pizzicato, muted, and double-stopping.
Styles of popular music often use different timbres.
The synthesiser creates a wide range of different sounds, including different synth leads, pads and basses.
keywords: when strings are played with a bow
a device that dampens and reduces the sound produced by an instrument
a string technique in which the performer plucks the string with a finger
a type of synthesised sound that is suited to playing melodies
a type of synthesised sound that is suited to playing sustained sounds

7453.name: Timbre around the world
7453.outcome: I can identify common instruments and timbres from a variety of musical traditions around the world.
points: There is a huge diversity of instruments around the world. Some have crossed between musical genres and traditions.
Common non-Western drums include tabla, timbales, conga, djembe and dhol.
There are many other important percussion instruments, including both tuned and untuned percussion.
There is also a diverse range of stringed instruments that can be heard.
These include guitar-like instruments like banjo, mandolin and bouzouki, and other instruments like tanpura and sarangi.
keywords: a guitar-like stringed instrument that has a distinct percussive ‘twangy’ timbre
a hand drum originating in Africa with a round, full timbre
a stringed instrument from the Indian subcontinent that creates a rich, ringing timbre with use of its resonant strings
a set of two drums on which the taal is played with the hands

7454.name: Vocal types, styles and techniques
7454.outcome: I can identify common voice types, styles and techniques.
points: Vocals are very diverse, with numerous voice types, styles and techniques.
An SATB choir is made up of the following female and male vocal types: soprano, alto, tenor and bass.
Some common vocal techniques include melisma, vibrato and rapping.
In some styles, microtonal singing, scat singing and beatboxing can also be heard.
keywords: a type of choir consisting of soprano, alto, tenor and bass singers
a vocal technique that imitates drum kit and percussion sounds
a technique in which male voices can sing much higher than their normal range; it has a distinct, thin, airy timbre
when there are syllables with more than one note sung to them
a vocal or instrumental technique in which the pitch ‘wobbles’ slightly

7455.name: The sounds of technology
7455.outcome: I can describe and identify the most common uses of music technology, including electronic sound production, sound effects and others.
points: Technology has hugely influenced the way that music is produced, edited and manipulated.
Synth pads, leads, basses and drum machines are common tools for producing sounds electronically.
Effects can be applied either live or after recording.
Some common effects are delay, reverb, chorus, auto-tune, distortion, panning and equalisation.
Overdubbing and DJing are two other important ways that technology has shaped modern music.
keywords: an effect that ‘echoes’ sounds back after a specific time
an instrument that synthesises drum sounds; the TR-808 is an example
adding new recorded sound to a pre-existing recording to create a combined effect
an effect that creates the impression of a sound being played in a more ‘echoey’ space
a DJing technique where the DJ creates a ‘wika wika’ sound by touching the record

7456.name: Understanding texture
7456.outcome: I can identify different textures and analyse interaction between instruments effectively.
points: Texture refers to both the number of different musical lines and the way that they relate to each other.
Common textures include monophonic, homophonic, unison, melody and accompaniment and polyphonic.
Other specific relationships between parts include contrary motion, imitation and harmonisation.
keywords: where two parts move in opposite directions (e.g. ascending and descending)
when one part plays at the same time as a melody, adding notes that create harmony with the melodic line
a texture consisting of a melody with a clearly separate accompaniment
a texture with more than one equally important melodic line
performing the same movement at exactly the same time as our partner

7457.name: Understanding metre
7457.outcome: I can identify simple, compound and irregular time signatures.
points: Time signatures (or metre) can be grouped into simple, compound and irregular time signatures.
Simple time signatures have two quavers in each beat.
Compound time signatures have three quavers in each beat.
Simple and compound time signatures can also be described as duple (2), triple (3) or quadruple (4 beats).
Irregular time signatures cannot be counted with groups of only 2 or only 3 beats. Examples are 7/8 and 5/4.
keywords: Compound time is when each beat is divided into three quavers, rather than two (e.g. a 12/8 time signature)
the number of beats cannot be divided by 2 or 3 (e.g. 5, 7)
each beat is divided into two quavers; 4/4 and 3/4 are examples of this

7458.name: Fundamentals of rhythm and tempo
7458.outcome: I can describe tempo accurately and can identify key rhythmic concepts by ear.
points: There are many different Italian terms to describe tempo, including largo, allegro and presto.
Tempo can also be measured in beats per minute (BPM).
Accelerando, ritardando and rubato change the tempo during a composition.
Some of the most common rhythmic features include syncopation, rhythmic motifs and cells and rhythmic repetition.
keywords: a rhythm that emphasises (accents) notes in between the main beats; this is often created by using half-beat rests on the beat or dotted rhythms
when the tempo gradually speeds up
a gradual slowing down of tempo; rallentando creates a similar effect
a slight speeding up and slowing down of the tempo to show expression
the first quaver in each pair has a slightly longer duration than the second quaver

7459.name: Other rhythmic concepts
7459.outcome: I can identify key rhythmic concepts, including anacrusis, polyrhythm, cross rhythms and hemiolas.
points: Many melodies use an anacrusis to start before beat one (the downbeat).
Polyrhythms include multiple rhythms that aren’t closely related playing together, creating a complex rhythmic texture.
Cross rhythms create the feeling of different pulses playing simultaneously.
A hemiola is used to create a brief effect of the pulse changing (by playing three notes over two beats or vice versa).
Diminution and augmentation develop rhythmic ideas by proportionally shortening or lengthening notes.
keywords: when a melody starts before the downbeat (beat 1)
a polyrhythm in which two or more of the rhythms 'conflict' and feel like they have a different pulse
the first and strongest beat of the bar
when three notes are played over the duration of two or vice versa, creating the feeling of tempo change
playing two or more conflicting rhythms at the same time

7460.name: Idiomatic rhythms around the world
7460.outcome: I can identify idiomatic rhythmic features of key Western and non-Western styles.
points: Many styles around the world are defined by idiomatic rhythms.
Some of these are linked with specific styles, such as skank (reggae), chaal (bhangra) and scotch snap (Celtic folk).
Others have their roots in specific regions, but are used in many styles, such as the clave and tresillo rhythms.
Some are not specific rhythms, but types of rhythms, such as swing, free rhythms and driving rhythms.
keywords: the name commonly given to a particular distinctive rhythm played on the dhol in bhangra
a five-note syncopated rhythm with various forms; the most common form is the son clave
fast, repeated rhythms that create a sense of energy
when free rhythms are played, they create no clear sense of pulse
a three-note rhythm that is the same as the ‘3’ of the son clave

7462.name: Understanding dynamics and articulation
7462.outcome: I can identify dynamics, dynamic changes and different types of articulation accurately.
points: Dynamics and articulation have a big impact on musical mood and character.
The most common dynamics are piano (p) and forte (f).
Dynamic changes are indicated with crescendo, diminuendo and subito (sudden) and poco a poco (little by little).
Staccato and legato (slurred) are the most common types of articulation.
Different kinds of articulation include accents, tenuto, marcato and sforzando.
keywords: a note that is emphasised, shown with this symbol: >
when the dynamics gradually decrease, getting quieter
a sudden, loud type of accent, marked with the abbreviation sfz
a note that is held for its full length, though still detached from surrounding notes

11834.name: Identifying rhythms
11834.outcome: I can accurately identify and notate four-beat rhythms.
points: Rhythmic dictation is the process of listening to a rhythm and writing it down using notation.
Verbalisation, using words to represent different note values and patterns, is a useful strategy for rhythmic dictation.
Words like ‘ta’ (crotchet) and ‘ta di’ (pair of quavers) can help to identify different note values.
We then convert those words into their correct notation symbols.
keywords: how long a note lasts for (for example, a crotchet has a note value of one beat)
the process of listening to a rhythm and writing it down
to express with words (for example, verbalising a rhythm is turning a rhythm into words)

11836.name: More complex rhythmic dictation
11836.outcome: I can accurately identify and notate complex rhythmic patterns.
points: Rhythmic dictation is slightly more complex with syncopated and dotted rhythms.
Identifying quaver rests (with ‘rest-di’) is useful for accurately notating syncopated rhythms.
In all time signatures we should make sure that the note values add up to the correct number of beats in a bar.
In compound time, we must carefully count groups of 3 quavers (using ‘1 and a 2 and a’ etc.)
keywords: Compound time is when each beat is divided into three quavers, rather than two (e.g. a 12/8 time signature)
a note that lasts for three quarters of a beat
a rhythm that emphasises (accents) notes in between the main beats; this is often created by using half-beat rests on the beat or dotted rhythms

11837.name: Identifying melodic shape
11837.outcome: I can identify the shape of a melody and represent it visually.
points: Identifying the shape of a melody is key to melodic dictation.
The melodic shape has to account for ascending and descending pitch, as well as conjunct and disjunct movement.
With disjunct intervals, we have to listen carefully to notice whether they are large or small leaps.
We can represent melodic shape using a line.
We can then approximate the correct pitches by drawing notes in to fit the rough melodic shape.
keywords: movement between notes based on small intervals (steps)
the process of listening to a melody and writing it down
movement between notes that involves intervals larger than two semitones (moving by leap)
the overall shape of a melody or part of a melody, including where it ascends or descends and where it is conjunct or disjunct

11838.name: Identifying intervals
11838.outcome: I can accurately identify a range of intervals by ear and notate them.
points: Identifying intervals is key to melodic dictation.
We can use reference melodies to help us identify specific intervals by comparing the interval to the specific melody.
We also need to consider whether an interval is ascending or descending.
Once we have worked out the interval, we can notate it by drawing it on the stave next to the given starting note.
keywords: A semitone is the smallest interval in most Western music (e.g. C to C#).
The general mood or feeling of a text.
the distance in pitch between two notes (e.g. a fifth)

11839.name: Developing pitch dictation skills
11839.outcome: I can notate consecutive intervals to complete pitch dictation accurately.
points: Notating a whole melody can be done by breaking it into a series of consecutive intervals.
Identify the melodic shape, then identify the first interval by singing it back and compare it to reference melodies.
Notate the first interval, then repeat for each consecutive interval.
Check your answer by matching it to the melodic shape visually and singing it back.
When given the rhythm, we should be careful to accurately copy it in the notated pitches.
keywords: A semitone is the smallest interval in most Western music (e.g. C to C#).
The general mood or feeling of a text.
the distance in pitch between two notes (e.g. a fifth)

11826.name: Describing melody, harmony, tonality and texture
11826.outcome: I can accurately describe the melody, harmony, tonality and texture of a piece of unfamiliar music.
points: We can use the musical elements to help structure simple, clear descriptions of unfamiliar music.
Accurate description of a melody should include its shape and intervals as well as any melodic devices.
A description of tonality should identify whether the music is diatonic (major or minor), modal, atonal or microtonal.
Harmony encompasses the types of chords used, harmonic rhythm, cadences and harmonic devices.
A description of texture should describe the specific texture (e.g. homophonic) and any changes that occur.
keywords: a pattern that uses the notes of an arpeggio (an ascending or descending broken chord)
composition techniques that affect the harmony, including pedals and modulations
specific techniques used in melodies, including ornamentation and sequences
a melody that uses segments of a scale
the type of notes and chords that a piece of music is based on (e.g. minor, major, atonal)

11829.name: Describing rhythm, tempo, timbre articulation and dynamics
11829.outcome: I can accurately describe the rhythm, tempo, timbre, articulation and dynamics of a piece of unfamiliar music.
points: A description of rhythm should mention specific note lengths or patterns, as well as any idiomatic rhythms.
A description of metre and tempo should use technical terms (e.g. presto) and identify tempo changes (e.g. rubato).
Timbre encompasses both the instruments that are used and the specific sounds or techniques used on them (e.g. muted).
Describing articulation and dynamics refers to how the note is played and how loud or soft the music is.
keywords: A metre is a standardised unit of measurement. We can abbreviate metre to m.
Articulation is how the note is played eg. legato, staccato or accented.
the description of the sound or tone of an instrument

11830.name: Describing unfamiliar music
11830.outcome: I can use my knowledge of all musical elements to write a detailed description of a piece of music.
points: The musical elements are a useful starting point for a description of unfamiliar music.
An effective description should encompass multiple different musical elements and should describe each in a concise way.
We can use the table method to help us structure our thoughts and arrange them into an effective paragraph.
We can also analyse the musical effect of those elements in the table.
Describing the effect of each feature gives a more thorough description of a piece of music.
keywords: the impact that a certain musical idea or device has, for example this could be creating a certain mood or feeling
the building blocks of music, which include rhythm, melody, harmony, structure and others

11831.name: Analysing musical purpose
11831.outcome: I can analyse how different elements have been used to achieve their musical purpose.
points: Most composers have a purpose in mind when they write music.
This might be to tell a story (e.g. programme music), create a mood or encourage dancing.
Composers use the musical elements in specific ways to suit the purpose of their music.
We can create a sophisticated description of music if we link the elements to the purpose of the music.
First we describe the element, then describe its effect, then analyse how that fits the purpose.
keywords: the building blocks of music, which include rhythm, melody, harmony, structure and others
what the piece of music is trying to achieve; this could be to represent something, encourage an action or create a mood or emotion
music that tells a story or creates an image of something

11832.name: Choosing elements and comparing music
11832.outcome: I can choose which elements to focus on in a musical description and can write an effective musical comparison.
points: The way we structure a description is dependent on the question.
If the question is linked to a particular style or context, every point must link to that.
If the question is linked to a musical purpose (e.g. depicting a specific scene) every point should link to that.
If it is a comparison, every feature that is described should be compared to the other clip.
Being concise, making only relevant points and using technical vocabulary are also key to effective responses.
keywords: the building blocks of music, which include rhythm, melody, harmony, structure and others
what the piece of music is trying to achieve; this could be to represent something, encourage an action or create a mood or emotion

1923.belief: The conductor is the only person responsible for keeping the pulse and pitch is only high and low.
1923.statement: The conductor is the only person responsible for keeping the pulse and pitch is only high and low.
1923.correction: The conductor can set the tempo but all performers are responsible for keeping the pulse in a performance. Pitch as high and low is slightly limiting. Help pupils make connections to other related words that they might know.

2268.belief: The description thick texture relates to the number of people performing and loud dynamics.
2268.statement: The description thick texture relates to the number of people performing and loud dynamics.
2268.correction: Texture is more complex than thick/thin. Use good examples early on to show that texture is related to the different layers in the music and not neccesarily the number of performers. Show how lots of performers could be performing in a thin texture.

2308.belief: We can develop a composition around any element of music.
2308.statement: We can develop a composition around any element of music.
2308.correction: Using the elements of music, particularly individually, is not always helpful for pupils to make a start on a composition. Finding a musical starting point such as a set of notes or rhythm allows pupils to then explore the elements through that idea.

9164.belief: The A sections in a musical structure which has a repeated A section have to be the same.
9164.statement: The A sections in a musical structure which has a repeated A section have to be the same.
9164.correction: Strong musical ideas usually have a balance of unity and variety, so even when a section is repeated, providing the main melodic idea is recognisable there can be some small changes which then helps to find this balance.

10115.belief: Taiko is the name of the style.
10115.statement: Taiko is the name of the style.
10115.correction: Taiko is Japanese for 'drum' and the drums make up kumi daiko which is ensemble drumming.

4738.belief: The movements and shouts are not related to the pulse and rhythm.
4738.statement: The movements and shouts are not related to the pulse and rhythm.
4738.correction: The movements and shouts, just like the drum strikes, are rhythmically important. Reinforce the pulse when teaching the movements, shouts and strikes.

4675.belief: Mixing up the dongo and doko strikes and comfortably swapping from one to the other.
4675.statement: Mixing up the dongo and doko strikes and comfortably swapping from one to the other.
4675.correction: The dongo is a shuffle feel, whilst the doko and kara are even beats. Practise alternating from one to the other so pupils can recognise them easily and can comfortably swap from one to the other in a performance.

2624.belief: All the elements have to be achieved perfectly in order to produce a successful taiko performance.
2624.statement: All the elements have to be achieved perfectly in order to produce a successful taiko performance.
2624.correction: There is a lot to consider when putting the performance together. Focus on playing and moving together with repeated ideas to start with. Working as a team and getting the count in and stance right is important to support the rest of the performance.

4666.belief: Mistaking F (or another note) for C and not understanding the impact this has on the finger prompts.
4666.statement: Mistaking F (or another note) for C and not understanding the impact this has on the finger prompts.
4666.correction: Reinforce 'C to the left of the two black keys', why F is a common mistake and the finger prompts only work if the C position is correct.

5286.belief: Overdoing the emphasis on the first note of the bar and the music becoming stilted.
5286.statement: Overdoing the emphasis on the first note of the bar and the music becoming stilted.
5286.correction: Play the pupils a non-example where the first beat is so strong it becomes unmusical and follow this with a good example.

8948.belief: Rhythm and pulse in music are the same thing (particularly as there are a lot of crotchets used).
8948.statement: Rhythm and pulse in music are the same thing (particularly as there are a lot of crotchets used).
8948.correction: Pupils could clap/tap the beat with the audio examples to reinforce how it is different to the rhythm of the melody..

6951.statement: Pupils misinterpret the score and think the accompaniment is the second line of the melody.
6951.correction: Encourage pupils to follow the score through when listening to the music and reinforce that both lines are part of the same system.

7285.statement: Pupils start playing on the snare because they are used to reading left to right.
7285.correction: Emphasise that the kick is the start because it is central within the drum kit.

8002.belief: The metronome matches the rhythms they play, since they previously played crotchets.
8002.statement: Pupils think the metronome matches the rhythms they play, since they previously played crotchets.
8002.correction: Pupils should play a metronome beat while the class claps quavers to highlight the metronome shows the pulse by clicking on the beats of the bar.

4667.belief: Misunderstanding the meaning of acoustic because the lesson examples are played on an iPad/computer.
4667.statement: Misunderstanding the meaning of acoustic because the lesson examples are played on an iPad/computer.
4667.correction: Make it clear that the iPad/computer is imitating acoustic sound.

8447.statement: Pupils try to record their new ideas into one of the pitched instrument tracks.
8447.correction: Demonstrate this error before they have time to improvise new ideas.

9645.belief: The string instruments can only be identified by pitch. The woodwind instruments are made of wood.
9645.statement: The string instruments can only be identified by pitch. The woodwind instruments are made of wood.
9645.correction: The pitch of the instruments does overlap slightly, so it's important to emphasise that the timbre of each instrument is slightly different. Most woodwind instruments were originally made of wood but the flute and the saxophone are now made of metal.

8570.statement: Pupils may use the number prompts but not find the correct C position on the keyboard.
8570.correction: Reinforce the position of the note C on the keyboard and ensure the pupils are sitting to play comfortably in the C position.

6964.statement: Pupils may mistake another note for F when changing position. Brass instruments can only be identified by pitch.
6964.correction: Reinforce that F is to the left of the three black keys; this has to be correct for the finger prompts to work. The ranges of the brass instruments overlap, so it's important to emphasise that the timbre of each instrument is slightly different.

4665.belief: Mistaking another note for F when changing position quickly. The timpani are untuned percussion because they are drums.
4665.statement: Mistaking another note for F when changing position quickly. The timpani are untuned percussion because they are drums.
4665.correction: Reinforce that F is to the left of the three black keys. Highlight that the timpani are tuned to specific pitches.

69.belief: The accompaniment part is semibreves throughout.
69.statement: The accompaniment part is semibreves throughout.
69.correction: Two bars of the accompaniment is in minims. Encourage pupils to practise this bar specifically on its own when putting both hands/parts together.

3444.belief: Both hands change position at the same time.
3444.statement: Both hands change position at the same time
3444.correction: Highlight to pupils that the left hand remains in the C position even though the right hand moves to the F position and back again.

1870.belief: Complicated rhythms will sound more interesting.
1870.statement: Complicated rhythms will sound more interesting.
1870.correction: Often creating simpler rhythms is more effective. In particular, rhythms that have rests (silence) in them can create a powerful contrast between sound and silence. Try using a mix of simple and complex rhythms.

5385.belief: The pentatonic scale is limited to one octave on the instrument.
5385.statement: The pentatonic scale is limited to one octave on the instrument.
5385.correction: The pentatonic scale is just the names of the notes that we can use. You can use them as high-pitched notes or low-pitched notes on your instrument. Experiment with playing the scale up high and down low.

10732.belief: Using the same rhythm in different ostinati creates effective contrast.
10732.statement: Using the same rhythm in different ostinati creates effective contrast.
10732.correction: Using different rhythms in your ostinati is important for creating contrast. If they use the same rhythm, they will inevitably sound very similar. Try coming up with some interesting rhythm by clapping, then play them using notes on the keyboard.

4312.belief: Lots of automation changes make the dynamics effective.
4312.statement: Lots of automation changes make the dynamics effective.
4312.correction: Doing lots of dynamic changes can sound chaotic and messy. Try to limit your use of automation so that changes are gradual and slowly change the dynamics.

3064.belief: Folk music all sounds the same.
3064.statement: Folk music all sounds the same.
3064.correction: Many folk traditions have shared characteristics, primarily because of the way that the music was passed between generations, but folk music is incredibly diverse, and covers lots of different types of music from different cultures and times.

3037.belief: You can fit any lyrics to a melody.
3037.statement: You can fit any lyrics to a melody.
3037.correction: Lyrics or melody often have to be adjusted to fit each other. This can be because there are too many or too few words to fit in a phrase, or there are too many or too few notes to fit with the words. Trial and error is the best way to address this.

2480.belief: The dorian mode is the same as a minor scale.
2480.statement: The dorian mode is the same as a minor scale.
2480.correction: There is a slight difference, with one different note. All of the modes are closely linked to major and minor scales, but have slightly different notes that help to create different moods.

9146.belief: Sea shanties are songs for pirates.
9146.statement: Sea shanties are songs for pirates.
9146.correction: Many cultures based around the sea use songs to coordinate movement on boats. Sea shanties are one example of this, and were sung by many, including sailors and fishermen. Other traditional cultures had their own songs for this purpose.

3441.belief: Hand positions should only change at the start of new phrases.
3441.statement: Hand positions should only change at the start of new phrases.
3441.correction: This depends entirely on what notes are used. Sometimes, like in Korobeiniki, it is more useful to change hand position during a phrase. When doing this, we should always practise making it seamless, so there is no obvious change in sound.

3063.belief: Folk dances and folk songs are different names for exactly the same thing.
3063.statement: Folk dances and folk songs are different names for exactly the same thing.
3063.correction: Not necessarily. Many folk songs are for storytelling or other purposes, not dancing. Some folk songs are designed for dancing, which often have different features, including an upbeat tempo, strong pulse and rhythmic drive.

4982.belief: Any note that precedes a strong beat is an upbeat.
4982.statement: Any note that precedes a strong beat is an upbeat.
4982.correction: An upbeat sounds like it musically belongs to the strong beat. Find a good non-example in a melody or drum groove to show how an upbeat both precedes the strong beat and also creates emphasis, often due to following a rest.

5580.belief: You can play an open hi-hat all the way through the bar or anywhere in the pattern.
5580.statement: You can play an open hi-hat all the way through the bar or anywhere in the pattern.
5580.correction: The hi-hat can be played open at any point, but it shouldn't be overused, and stylistically it works well on the last quaver or off the beat.

2519.belief: Drum fills must be more complex than the fundamental groove.
2519.statement: Drum fills must be more complex than the fundamental groove.
2519.correction: Show how absence of sound can be as powerful as added sound by giving an example of the groove briefly stopping.

10345.belief: Toms are only used in fills. Use of the snare/claps/clicks will automatically be a backbeat.
10345.statement: Toms are only used in fills. Use of the snare/claps/clicks will automatically be a backbeat.
10345.correction: Toms can be used in the main groove just less commonly than the kick/snare. For a backbeat the snare/claps have to play on beats 2 and 4.

5522.belief: Any pitch and notes can work in a composition.
5522.statement: Any pitch and notes can work in a composition.
5522.correction: Encourage pupils to think about the choice of notes in their musical ideas and listen to how it sounds.

904.belief: Certain timbres can only be used for certain effects.
904.statement: Certain timbres can only be used for certain effects.
904.correction: Some timbres are particularly well suited to certain moods or effects but this doesn't mean that other timbres can't be used for different effects. It can also depend on the other musical features used.

10758.belief: Using all the white notes is C major will sound cheerful.
10758.statement: Using all the white notes is C major will sound cheerful
10758.correction: It's important that the home note (in this case C) is used appropriately to reinforce the notes sounding like they are in C major.

914.belief: You can only change the 3rd or the 6th of the scale to change the mood of the music.
914.statement: You can only change the 3rd or the 6th of the scale to change the mood of the music.
914.correction: In the lesson task any suitable chromatic movement can be used to change the feel of the motif, so pupils don't explicitly have to change the 3rd and the 6th. Play a range of motifs in the major key and change different notes so pupils can see this.

9456.belief: A soundtrack should have music all the way through.
9456.statement: A soundtrack should have music all the way through.
9456.correction: Careful use of silence can heighten the tension and help to emphasise the dialogue. There is a balance and silence can be used sparingly to elevate other parts of the music and the story, particularly after a musical build up.

9190.belief: A sense of style in music refers only to the genre.
9190.statement: A sense of style in music refers only to the genre.
9190.correction: Style can mean genre-specific features but also can refer to compositional style and the composer using common features throughout a particular piece.

10601.belief: You must use the given rhythms.
10601.statement: You must use the given rhythms.
10601.correction: The rhythms used are variations on traditional accompaniments that are passed down orally across generations. At this stage, any rhythm can be used as a starting point for getting pupils making music but this example covers the required techniques.

8945.belief: The rhythm is the definitive version of the Kuku rhythm.
8945.statement: The rhythm is the definitive version of the Kuku rhythm.
8945.correction: There are different versions of this piece from both Guinea and the Ivory Coast. There are also local versions within each of these. This version is a guide and can be adapted to suit your local context.

9410.belief: The solo section has to be made up in the moment.
9410.statement: The solo section has to be made up in the moment.
9410.correction: The solo section can use ideas that are already planned. This is a good starting point for adding solos to build confidence and then build up to doing improvised ideas.

10083.belief: Swapping comfortably and accurately from one rhythm to another with the overall structure.
10083.statement: Swapping comfortably and accurately from one rhythm to another with the overall structure.
10083.correction: This is quite tricky as the strucutre is complex. Break it down for pupils so they learn each section comfortably and encourage them to practise going from one rhythm to the next and think about strategies for remembering the rhythms.

3673.belief: Improvisation means making something up from nothing.
3673.statement: Improvisation means making something up from nothing
3673.correction: You can use typical rhythms or features of the style as a basis oof any improvisation. This might mean using an establisehd idea such as a prepared triplet or syncopated rhtyhm and then extending the idea with something made up in the moment.

1879.belief: Composing a rhyhtm means creating something totally original.
1879.statement: Composing a rhyhtm means creating something totally original
1879.correction: Successful compositions often take some ideas from other pieces and do something new with it, so adapting rhythms from the drumming pieces you have already played is acceptable and can help in finding the right type of rhythms and the right style.

522.belief: The backbeat and off-beat are the same.
522.statement: The backbeat and off-beat are the same.
522.correction: The backbeat is on beat 2 and 4 while the off-beat is on the second half of a beat (in between the beats).

8947.belief: If a rhythm includes quavers it is syncopated.
8947.statement: If a rhythm includes quavers it is syncopated.
8947.correction: This is a common misconception when first learning syncopation. Reiterate that a rhythm is only syncopated if the emphasis is in between the main beats. In practice here, that means that there will be a quaver rest at the start of a beat.

4315.belief: Having lots of layers of music playing simultaneously is effective use of texture.
4315.statement: Having lots of layers of music playing simultaneously is effective use of texture.
4315.correction: It is easy to create a texture that is too thick and too busy. Encourage students to experiment with both thin and thick textures and reiterate that adding too many layers simultaneously can make music sound ineffective.

164.belief: Adjusting EQ and/or dynamics is always musically beneficial.
164.statement: Adjusting EQ and/or dynamics is always musically beneficial.
164.correction: Encourage students to use the DAW tools sparingly and reinforce the point that these tools are effective but that it is possible to overuse them. The analogy of seasoning on a meal - too much can spoil the meal - can be an effective one to use.

5599.belief: Playing the sequence incorrectly, particularly missing the final F in the sequence.
5599.statement: Playing the sequence incorrectly, particularly missing the final F in the sequence.
5599.correction: Encourage pupils to learn the chord structure from memory and to think in 4-bar phrases. Highlight the last phrase specifically which has two chord changes.

3815.belief: All instruments have a fixed role and only the drums drive the music forward.
3815.statement: All instruments have a fixed role and only the drums drive the music forward.
3815.correction: The guitar and piano can be melodic as well as accompanying. Different instruments can drive the music forward, and all players in the ensemble are responsible for this.

4980.belief: Any note of the boogie-woogie pattern can rise and fall.
4980.statement: Any note of the boogie-woogie pattern can rise and fall.
4980.correction: Whilst there are different variations of boogie-woogie, it is important that pupils keep the root the same and the 5th of the chord rises and falls.

787.belief: The C blues scale can use any of the black notes (flattened notes) on the keyboard.
787.statement: The C blues scale can use any of the black notes (flattened notes) on the keyboard.
787.correction: The blues scale uses specific flattened notes - 3rd, 5th and 7th. It's important for pupils to practise finding these notes and getting used to how the scale sounds.

3674.belief: Improvisation means the notes are chosen at random.
3674.statement: Improvisation means the notes are chosen at random.
3674.correction: Although improvising means making music up on the spot, it is based on a set of notes or scale and can use repetition. Improvisation often uses fixed stylistic characteristics such as particular rhythms, phrase structures and chord sequences.

4988.belief: Any notes will work for improvising.
4988.statement: Any notes will work for improvising
4988.correction: Find the balance between developing confidence in improvising and quality of musical ideas. Encourage pupils to think about the choice of notes, repetition, returning to a main note etc, as well as trying ideas and reflecting on what they sound like.

127.belief: Adjacent white notes on the keyboard are all a tone apart.
127.statement: Adjacent white notes on the keyboard are all a tone apart.
127.correction: Most of the adjacent white notes are a tone apart but because of the pattern of the black notes on the keyboard some of the adjacent white notes are also semitones. It's important for pupils to count the notes to work out an interval.

9027.belief: The more rubato you use the more expressive the performance.
9027.statement: The more rubato you use the more expressive the performance
9027.correction: Rubato affects the tempo and pulse of a piece so needs to be used with subtlety. Show various examples of how Fur Elise might be played by different performers so pupils can see the variety of ways rubato can be used.

8857.belief: Related keys are those with the same home (tonic) note such as C major and C minor.
8857.statement: Related keys are those with the same home (tonic) note such as C major and C minor.
8857.correction: Related keys are those with the same notes, but a different home (tonic note). Major and minor scales have different tone and semitone patterns, so they need to start three semitones apart for the notes to be the same.

9189.belief: Sense of pulse and sense of rhythm are the same thing.
9189.statement: Sense of pulse and sense of rhythm are the same thing
9189.correction: A sense of pulse is understanding the underlying beat in the music. A sense of rhythm is understanding where the stress should be in a bar or rhythm. This is much more nuanced. At this point, encourage pupils to stress the downbeat.

8817.belief: When we refer to the A section of a piece of music (in relation to structure) they have to be exactly the same.
8817.statement: When we refer to the A section of a piece of music (in relation to structure) they have to be exactly the same.
8817.correction: Letters are used to describe sections overall but quite often there are slight differences. Use some common examples of songs pupils will know of where sections might be labelled the same piece of music, but where there are small differences.

70.belief: The accompaniment patterns for section A and section B are the same and the best way to practise is to play from the start to the end of the piece repeatedly.
70.statement: The accompaniment patterns for section A and section B are the same and the best way to practise is to play from the start to the end of the piece repeatedly.
70.correction: The accompaniment pattern changes slightly in section B. Highlight the difference so pupils are sure of this when practising hands together. It's more efficient to identify and practise the difficult bars in isolation first.

10430.belief: The tresillo ('triplet' in Spanish) uses three equally spaced notes.
10430.statement: The tresillo ('triplet' in Spanish) uses three equally spaced notes.
10430.correction: The notes in the tresillo rhythm are not equally spaced. The third note is a shorter duration. Counting the semiquavers in a 3-3-2 pattern can help us space the notes correctly (1-2-3, 1-2-3, 1-2).

3823.belief: An interesting, developed dembow beat should be complex.
3823.statement: An interesting, developed dembow beat should be complex.
3823.correction: Often keeping things simple is more effective than complexity. Choose one or two of the suggested ways of developing your drum beat, rather than trying to add everything in.

4546.belief: Any melodic idea that repeats is a hook.
4546.statement: Any melodic idea that repeats is a hook.
4546.correction: It's a bit more complex than that. In some cases, whether something is a hook or not could be a matter of opinion, not necessarily true or false. A hook must be short, memorable, and repeated.

3650.belief: It is important to constantly create variety and change in a composition.
3650.statement: It is important to constantly create variety and change in a composition.
3650.correction: We have to balance variety and repetition. Too much variety makes a piece sound messy and incoherent, too much repetition and it becomes boring. Try to find a happy medium between repeating ideas and varying things (e.g. the texture).

10138.belief: Tall vowels mean singing louder or just opening the mouth really wide.
10138.statement: Tall vowels mean singing louder or just opening the mouth really wide.
10138.correction: Although they do help with projection, tall vowels are not about volume, they’re about the vertical space inside the mouth. If the mouth is too wide horizontally (grinning), this can tense the jaw, leading to a strained tone.

3333.belief: Good balance means the parts should be the same volume all the time.
3333.statement: Good balance means the parts should be the same volume all the time.
3333.correction: There is a nuance to balance and we always need to listen to other performers in the ensemble to check we can hear them and particularly hear the lead line. In Gumama all parts are of equal importance so the parts are a similar volume.

10098.belief: Syncopation always makes music sound more energetic and driving.
10098.statement: Syncopation always makes music sound more energetic and driving.
10098.correction: Syncopation can make a piece feel laid back by relaxing the timing to give a 'behind the beat' effect. Syncopated rhythms often leave gaps between sounds, which can make the groove feel more spacious and less rushed.

104.belief: To add shape to a melody, the emphasis will always be on the first note of the phrase.
104.statement: To add shape to a melody, the emphasis will always be on the first note of the phrase.
104.correction: This is not always the case. Quite often, when the first note of the phrase lands on the downbeat this is naturally where the emphasis falls, however, this is more about where the main beats are rather than where the phrase starts.

788.belief: C position is thumb on C in the left hand.
788.statement: C position is thumb on C in the left hand.
788.correction: The C position is when the hand is placed in a position to play C up to G. With the right hand, this would be the thumb on C, finger 2 on D etc. With the left hand, the C position is when the little finger is on C, finger 4 is on D etc.

3405.belief: A ground bass pattern should finish on the tonic as it 'sounds' finished.
3405.statement: A ground bass pattern should finish on the tonic as it 'sounds' finished.
3405.correction: The final bar of the piece should finish on the tonic note, but until that bar, the pattern wants to repeat. Finishing on the dominant or the leading note naturally helps the music return to the first note of the pattern, which should be the tonic.

111.belief: When adding chords to a bass line, the chord has to be the same as the note in the bass.
111.statement: When adding chords to a bass line, the chord has to be the same as the note in the bass.
111.correction: In most cases the bass note should be one of the notes in the chord, but doesn't always have to be the lowest note of the chord. For a balanced chord sequence most notes in the bass lines should be the root, but not all have to be.

209.belief: An Alberti bass is the notes of the triad played in any order.
209.statement: An Alberti bass is the notes of the triad played in any order.
209.correction: An Alberti bass has a specfic, distinctive pattern which uses the lowest note, highest note, middle note, highest note of the triad in that order.

5140.belief: One iteration of the tresillo and habanera has to last for two beats.
5140.statement: One iteration of the tresillo and habanera has to last for two beats.
5140.correction: The tresillo and habanera can be played in 2/4 or 4/4. The important thing is the relationship of the notes to each other. Practise clapping the rhythms twice as fast or slow to the same beat to help pupils grasp this concept.

3842.belief: An interval of a 3rd is three tones higher or lower than the first note.
3842.statement: An interval of a 3rd is three tones higher or lower than the first note.
3842.correction: In C major (where pupils are counting the white keys), they should count the starting note and final note, plus any in between. So an interval of a 3rd is actually two tones higher or lower than the first note. An octave would be seven notes higher.

3041.belief: There is a fixed and correct finger pattern for performing keyboard pieces.
3041.statement: There is a fixed and correct finger pattern for performing keyboard pieces.
3041.correction: With pieces that require a dexterous hand postition change, there are often several options. Encourage pupils to find a comfortable solution. Show examples of good keyboard technique that allows them to perform more difficult melodies with control.

4770.belief: Music for films is always recorded and played through speakers.
4770.statement: Music for films is always recorded and played through speakers.
4770.correction: Before technology existed to do this, film music was played live by performers in the room. It would often be a solo piano/organ player, who would improvise along with the film. Sometimes, ensembles such as orchestras would play music live instead.

2387.belief: A diminished seventh chord is just like any other extended chord - a triad with added notes.
2387.statement: A diminished seventh chord is just like any other extended chord - a triad with added notes.
2387.correction: A diminished seventh chord is quite unique as every interval is the same size (three semitones). It is different from extended chords that add notes to a triad. It has been used for centuries as a tense, dramatic chord, including in silent movies.

5511.belief: When a piano player plays music with a silent movie it is always completely improvised.
5511.statement: When a piano player plays music with a silent movie it is always completely improvised.
5511.correction: While they improvise many aspects, they often use specific musical ideas to create specific effects. This includes vamps, certain chords (e.g. diminished 7th for tension) and musical clichés like the misterioso that create certain effects.

4098.belief: A leitmotif and a film theme are the same thing.
4098.statement: A leitmotif and a film theme are the same thing.
4098.correction: Not quite. Many films have themes that represent the overall mood, and can be heard throughout the film. The difference with a leitmotif is that it explicitly represents one thing - a character, place or an idea.

9301.belief: Simply changing the instrument makes a leitmotif change mood.
9301.statement: Simply changing the instrument makes a leitmotif change mood.
9301.correction: While it does have an impact, changing other elements can make this even greater. Harmony, rhythm, dynamics, articulation and tempo are particularly useful for motivic transformation.

5348.belief: All of the parts are necessary to make the project work.
5348.statement: All of the parts are necessary to make the project work.
5348.correction: Ideally pupils will record in all of the parts of the batucada, but the project will still work successfully with the core ensemble of surdo, caixa and repinique.

5144.belief: There is only one note that can be added to create a seventh chord, and likewise for a sixth chord.
5144.statement: There is only one note that can be added to create a seventh chord, and likewise for a sixth chord.
5144.correction: There are various different types of sixth and seventh chords, which have different rules about how to form them. Here we are just learning the general principle of forming extended chords.

556.belief: The bass line must have a different rhythm from the chords and percussion parts.
556.statement: The bass line must have a different rhythm from the chords and percussion parts.
556.correction: It can be appropriate for the bass line to use the same rhythm as another part. If it sounds effective then it is fine.

8965.correction: While there are rules that help us improvise effectively, a big part of learning to improvise is experimenting and seeing what works and what doesn't. Be willing to make 'mistakes' and don't fixate on doing it perfectly first time.

3490.belief: Only highly skilled and naturally gifted musicians can work out music by ear.
3490.statement: Only highly skilled and naturally gifted musicians can work out music by ear.
3490.correction: Anyone can work out music by ear. It just takes practice and is made easier through use of effective strategies, including working out rhythm and pitch separately, and identifying individual pitches through trial and error.

2521.belief: All drum grooves have exactly the same rhythms in the kick, snare and hi-hat.
2521.statement: All drum grooves have exactly the same rhythms in the kick, snare and hi-hat.
2521.correction: Many typical drum grooves do have the same features or features very close to this, however encourage pupils to identify where there are subtle differences and how the kick, snare and hi-hat patterns can be varied within these features.

10101.belief: Synthesisers are most effective for melodic lines.
10101.statement: Synthesisers are most effective for melodic lines.
10101.correction: Different types of synthesiser suit different musical roles. While synth leads are very effective for melodic lines, synth pads are well-suited to playing accompaniments, particularly sustained notes and chords.

557.belief: Bass parts are normally simple and just play the lowest notes from the chords.
557.statement: Bass parts are normally simple and just play the lowest notes from the chords.
557.correction: In some cases this is true, but in many cases bass lines are interesting patterns and can often be defining features of songs. This is true for both Under Pressure and Feel Good Inc.

2358.belief: Different voice types cannot sing any of the same notes.
2358.statement: Different voice types cannot sing any of the same notes.
2358.correction: The ranges of voices overlap, so there are some notes that can be sung by different voice types. For example, many notes that a bass can sing are also possible for tenor voices to sing.

3554.belief: The human voice can only produce one note at a time.
3554.statement: The human voice can only produce one note at a time.
3554.correction: Every sound we make has multiple different notes, its just that the main note is much louder than the others. Think about when you have a croaky voice - it almost sounds like multiple notes, because it is! Multiphonics just amplify the quieter notes.

9082.correction: This is not true - a sample is any pre-existing sound that is used in a new way. This could be traditionally non-musical sounds like machinery or speech, or it could be clips of pieces of music or individual notes.

4787.belief: Only musical instruments (and voices) produce pitched sound.
4787.statement: Only musical instruments (and voices) produce pitched sound.
4787.correction: Pitched sounds are everywhere. In fact, most sounds have a pitch, it is often just hard to hear it. You can probably hear a pitched sound now if you listen closely - electrical buzzing, distant speech, weather or animals all produce subtle pitches.

10349.belief: A tone row is just a scale.
10349.statement: A tone row is just a scale.
10349.correction: A tone row is different because it isn't just a set of notes to choose from, but a specific order. When you are composing something in C major, you can use the notes of the C major scale in any order. With a tone row, they have a specific order.

8931.belief: Retrograding breaks the rules of serialism because it changes the order of the notes.
8931.statement: Retrograding breaks the rules of serialism because it changes the order of the notes.
8931.correction: Serialist composers don't consider retrograding breaking the rules. It does change the order, but the new order is still closely linked to the original tone row (by being reversed). It is therefore an acceptable and musically interesting technique.

8986.belief: Rock is a specific, narrow genre in itself.
8986.statement: Rock is a specific, narrow genre in itself.
8986.correction: Rock is a very broad term for lots of different musical genres, spanning a wide range of influences and using very different musical features. There are many sub-genres of rock, including grunge, punk rock and heavy metal.

2520.belief: Drum fills have to be complex and use lots of different parts of the drum kit. The tom-toms can be played in any order.
2520.statement: Drum fills have to be complex and use lots of different parts of the drum kit. The tom-toms can be played in any order.
2520.correction: Drum fills can be effective using only one or two parts of the kit, such as the snare and kick. The key is that they have a distinct rhythm that separates them from the main drum groove. When using the toms, they should be played from high to low.

5747.belief: Power chords are any two notes of the chord triad.
5747.statement: Power chords are any two notes of the chord triad.
5747.correction: For a chord to be a power chord it has to be the root and the fifth, not the root and the third. It also needs to be a perfect fifth. If pupils are working out their own power chords on the keyboard, some chords would use the black notes.

2831.belief: Not everyone can write a good melody.
2831.statement: Not everyone can write a good melody.
2831.correction: Writing a melody is just like writing a paragraph. Break it into small chunks (phrases). If you are finding it difficult to create a phrase, keep it simple and start by just improvising using 2 or 3 notes.

3454.belief: Harmonic rhythm means the rhythm that each chord plays.
3454.statement: Harmonic rhythm means the rhythm that each chord plays.
3454.correction: Harmonic rhythm means how often the chords change, not the actual rhythm that the chords play. Show examples of the same harmonic rhythm different rhythms in the chords. Changing the harmonic rhythm is a useful tool to alter the feel of music.

9323.belief: Singing a melody is only possible if you are a very strong singer.
9323.statement: Singing a melody is only possible if you are a very strong singer.
9323.correction: Everyone can sing, but keeping to a small range of notes can help when building confidence with singing. Singing helps us to internalise the notes and really 'feel' the melody. Melodies can sound much more natural when sung.

539.belief: The balance is the same throughout a song.
539.statement: The balance is the same throughout a song.
539.correction: The balance changes depending on the parts and texture. The melody line would usually be the most prominent part. In an accompaniment texture all parts are more likely to be equal. It's important to listen and be aware of the lead line.

3098.belief: Forgetting to listen to each other at the end of phrases and changing from one part to another.
3098.statement: Forgetting to listen to each other at the end of phrases and changing from one part to another.
3098.correction: Explain where pupils finish the longer notes together. They may pick a lot of this up from listening, but reinforce the importance of this in a powerful performance. Rehearse the changes from section to section to develop confidence in this.

7561.belief: When pupils take a big breath, they raise their shoulders.
7561.statement: When pupils take a big breath, they raise their shoulders.
7561.correction: A singing breath is from the diaphragm; the upper body and shoulders should remain relaxed.

2336.belief: Diction (articulation) is just about clear pronunciation.
2336.statement: Diction (articulation) is just about clear pronunciation.
2336.correction: Articulation is also connected to taking suitable singing breaths. If breathing is poorly controlled, consonants can sound weak or unclear, and vowels lose focus. Good breath support allows the voice to stay energised through quick or complex lyrics.

10100.correction: You can use a synthesiser if you have one or show a youtube clip of one in action. Use keyboard and different sounds to explain synthesised

3527.belief: Hooks and riffs are the same thing.
3527.statement: Hooks and riffs are the same thing.
3527.correction: A riff is the more important feature in how the song fits together and tends to underpin some of the main sections in the music. It is also a more suitable musical starting point for a pop song composition.

1651.belief: Chord sequences have to follow fixed rules exactly.
1651.statement: Chord sequences have to follow fixed rules exactly.
1651.correction: We use parameters as a guide to give a musical starting point for composing, but sometimes you might find other chords work. Always encourage pupils to try out a few ideas and perform their ideas so they can hear what they sound like.

8951.belief: The rhythm section 'plays the rhythm'. Rhythm sections are a fixed group of instruments.
8951.statement: The rhythm section 'plays the rhythm'. Rhythm sections are a fixed group of instruments.
8951.correction: Highlight the roles of the band and how they 'support' the singer and don't just provide rhythm for the song. There is some flexibility in the rhythm section. Not all the instruments have to be present in the music all of the time.

4786.belief: For musical ideas, such as a riff or melody to contrast, they have to be totally different.
4786.statement: For musical ideas, such as a riff or melody to contrast, they have to be totally different.
4786.correction: Songs should have to have some continuity between the different sections. Highlight ways in which two melodically different ideas might still have some similarities ie. same rhythm, same shape, same number of notes, same initial motif.

10717.belief: Using new ideas in every bar is the best way to compose a melody.
10717.statement: Using new ideas in every bar is the best way to compose a melody
10717.correction: Finding a balance of repetition and variety is usually more successful as it helps the melody become memorable.

4549.belief: A melody must feature a motif.
4549.statement: A melody must feature a motif.
4549.correction: This is not necessarily true - great melodies do not have to use motifs. However, they are a useful feature to understand when learning to write melodies, because they encourage composers to balance repetition anc contrast effectively.

9158.correction: Secondary chords are important for interesting harmony and using them is a good idea. As you become a more experienced composer, you'll learn how to effectively use them. For now, a good rule of thumb is to use them sparingly.

10687.belief: Using chord inversions for every chord will make the chord sequence more interesting.
10687.statement: Using chord inversions for every chord will make the chord sequence more interesting.
10687.correction: Using some inversions can make the chord sequence more interesting, but too many can sound unusual. Starting and finishing with a root position chord can help to reinforce the key.

4548.belief: A melody must be completely conjunct.
4548.statement: A melody must be completely conjunct.
4548.correction: This is not true - great melodies often use disjunct movement. However, when learning to compose melodies, sticking to mostly conjunct movement and small intervals helps them to sound melodic.

10688.belief: Using chords from within a minor key creates a dark mood.
10688.statement: Using chords from within a minor key creates a dark mood.
10688.correction: It's more complex than that - it is important to carefully choose which chords within the key you emphasise to create a dark mood. Emphasising chord i and other minor chords helps to make it feel dark and ominous, rather than any chords from the key.

3230.belief: The genre of the music tells us exactly what kind of film it is.
3230.statement: The genre of the music tells us exactly what kind of film it is.
3230.correction: This is not always true. Sometimes composers deliberately use genres that go against expectations. This might be for humour, or to create a strange clash. A good example would be A Knight's Tale, which uses modern genres in a medieval film.

4097.belief: A leimotif is just a musical theme.
4097.statement: A leimotif is just a musical theme.
4097.correction: Not quite. A leitmotif is a musical idea that must represent something else. This is usually a character, place or idea. A musical theme can exist without representing anything at all.

5128.belief: One feature on its own will make a leitmotif have a particular mood.
5128.statement: One feature on its own will make a leitmotif have a particular mood.
5128.correction: The mood of a leitmotif comes from a combination of different musical elements, including melodic features. Changing one feature might slightly change the mood, but to create a strong mood you need to consider all different aspects of the leitmotif.

2093.belief: To create a contrasting version of a leitmotif, you should change lots of features of it.
2093.statement: To create a contrasting version of a leitmotif, you should change lots of features of it.
2093.correction: You must be careful to not change it too much. If you do, it becomes unrecognisable and will just sound like a different leitmotif. A leitmotif represents a character, place, or idea, so we need to be able to recognise it to link it to that thing.

1661.belief: Chromatic and atonal are the same thing.
1661.statement: Chromatic and atonal are the same thing.
1661.correction: Atonal music sounds chromatic, because there is no clear tonal centre. However, chromatic music isn't necessarily atonal - a piece can be in a key, but use chromatic notes from outside of it.

683.belief: Black notes are the same thing as chromatic notes.
683.statement: Black notes are the same thing as chromatic notes.
683.correction: This is not always true. Chromatic notes are any notes that are from outside of the key. If you are in C major, which only uses white notes, the black notes will be chromatic. However, in other keys the black notes might not be chromatic.

8892.belief: Repetitive film music is not very interesting and can't build excitement.
8892.statement: Repetitive film music is not very interesting and can't build excitement.
8892.correction: Music that repeats ideas can build excitement if the composer develops aspects of it. By adding layers, changing rhythms and developing the texture, a simple repeated idea can be developed into an exciting musical soundworld.

2975.belief: All film music has to be precise to the second to fit the action perfectly.
2975.statement: All film music has to be precise to the second to fit the action perfectly.
2975.correction: Some film scenes do have to be exact where the music mirrors precisely what is happening on screen, but much film music is about creating the correct atmosphere and feel and this can be just as important when composing programmatic music.

929.belief: Changes between moods in a scene should always be sudden.
929.statement: Changes between moods in a scene should always be sudden.
929.correction: This is not always the case. Sometimes it is more appropriate to create a gradual change so that the shift isn't dramatically obvious. This might be where there is a gradual change of mood or action in a scene.

698.belief: Blues is an old style of music that isn't relevant anymore.
698.statement: Blues is an old style of music that isn't relevant anymore.
698.correction: While it's true that blues first developed more than a century ago, it continued to be an important style all through the 20th century and up to the present day. It shaped many different styles (including rock) that came to be incredibly important.

590.belief: Because rock 'n' roll often uses the 12-bar blues, this means it is just a type of blues.
590.statement: Because rock 'n' roll often uses the 12-bar blues, this means it is just a type of blues.
590.correction: Many styles use the 12-bar blues, including pop, rock, jazz and other styles. While rock 'n' roll is closely related to blues, its defining features are quite different, and its role as a commerical pop style is far from the origins of blues.

10546.belief: Unison and homophonic textures are the same thing and unison parts have to be played in the same octave.
10546.statement: Unison and homophonic textures are the same thing and unison parts have to be played in the same octave.
